pending_items.title: Gaza’s chess players survive a genocide and rebuild a community
pending_items.content:
Gaza City – Raghad Rabie, 18, never expected to beat her chess coach, Raghad Adas, at chess. During the friendly match, Rabie deliberately left some of her pieces exposed to distract her opponent as she planned a move that would deliver a checkmate in two turns.

Her strategy worked, giving her confidence in her abilities as a chess player. But the match also reflected something bigger: The return of chess to Gaza after the Israeli genocide devastated sporting activities across the enclave.

Rabie began learning chess in August 2025, when she was displaced in southern Gaza. Looking for something new to learn and a way to occupy her time, she taught herself the basic rules online before joining a training course run by Adas.

“I had admired chess players for a long time and wanted to learn the game. I started on my own, then the course helped me improve,” she says.

She has since participated in two tournaments and dreams of becoming a chess grandmaster, the goal of every serious chess player, and representing Palestine internationally.

But pursuing that ambition in Gaza, still under an Israeli siege and subject to daily air attacks despite an October 2025 “ceasefire”, is difficult.

There is no permanent training venue for chess players, so weekly gatherings take place in different locations, including the Lord Cafe in the al-Rimal neighbourhood of Gaza City.

To become an International Chess Federation (FIDE)-rated grandmaster, as Rabie hopes, requires thousands of hours of dedicated practice and study. But a shortage of chessboards, clocks and chess books – and soaring prices for any available chess equipment – has made this mission difficult.

Before the war, Adas was captain of the girls’ Spark team, playing in Palestinian Chess Federation tournaments. She was also among 10 players selected to take part in matches against other Palestinians from the occupied West Bank with the goal of forming a national team, which it was hoped would compete internationally.

Travel arrangements and permit procedures had been completed, but then Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza broke out in October 2023, killing at least 74,000 Palestinians and laying waste to the Palestinian enclave.

“I was excited about taking part in an international tournament, but the war made everything much more difficult,” Adas told Al Jazeera.

Adas said the team’s headquarters was destroyed, its players were scattered across Gaza, and she lost contact with several former teammates amid the forced Israeli displacements.

About a year after the war began, Adas started teaching chess in shelters, initially volunteering before working with organisations and eventually continuing her mission independently. She noticed a growing interest in the sport among newcomers, as well as the return of players who had stopped playing during the genocide.

This led her to establish “Stalemate” in February, a community chess initiative that began with 12 players and now boasts 470 members in its messaging group. Not all are active players; some are still learning or following its activities, but weekly get-togethers typically still attract between 20 and 40 participants.

These include children, young people, women and older players. Adas said she has noticed that the events have given people traumatised by the genocide a reason to leave their homes and meet other people again.

“I wanted chess to become a space that brings people together, rather than remaining a game limited to professionals or people who frequent cafes,” she said.

Stalemate has organised several competitive events, including an individual tournament on November 19 in Gaza City, which attracted 41 players. The competition consisted of nine rounds using the Swiss system to allow players to compete against players of a similar level.

Sharif Daher, deputy head of the Palestinian Chess Federation, said Gaza had more than 500 chess players before the war, including at least 200 regular players and about 20 clubs participating in local competitions.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has severely affected players and the venues where they used to meet and compete.

Nelly al-Masri, a federation member and spokesperson, said the destruction of sport facilities has made restarting activities extremely difficult, and the problems faced by Palestinians in Gaza run much deeper than returning to play the sport.

“The sport infrastructure in Gaza has been destroyed. The situation has become catastrophic and requires humanitarian relief work, not sports activities,” she told Al Jazeera.

Nevertheless, at the request of players, the federation has resumed training sessions and tournaments, despite limited funding, equipment and difficulties travelling between northern and southern Gaza, with Israel still strictly controlling movement.

The federation’s first official competition in Gaza since the war began was the aptly named “Return and Loyalty Tournament” in January 2026, which attracted more than 50 players. In June, the federation organised the Gaza Open Rapid Chess Championship, with 84 participants, followed in July by the eighth Musa Issa Saba Memorial Rapid Chess Championship, which attracted 92 players.

These tournaments helped bring former players back to the sport while introducing new faces to chess. However, the federation also lost players during the war, including member Walid Abu al-Hassan, a local chess champion who was killed along with his wife and two children in an Israeli air raid on their tent in Khan Younis in 2024.

Among those who have continued playing is 24-year-old Anas al-Rifi, who began learning chess in 2023 after a friend introduced him to the movement of the pieces on the board.

He developed his skills through YouTube tutorials, playing against more experienced opponents and learning from his mistakes.

Al-Rifi says he reached a rating of 2,000 on Chess.com on November 25, 2026. While this is not an official rating of FIDE, the sport’s official governing body, it is still in the top 1 percent of users of the hugely popular online chess platform.

Chess, he says, gives him a chance to temporarily distance himself from the harrowing circumstances around him.

“When I sit in front of the board and the clock starts counting down, my mind becomes calm. I think about nothing except the next move,” he told Al Jazeera.

With electronic chess clocks now a rarity in Gaza, some gatherings rely on a limited number of devices or mobile phone applications to keep track of game timings.

Khalil Baroud, who owns a small bookstore in Gaza City’s Nassr neighbourhood, said the Israeli siege on Gaza – which has restricted the import of most items used by the population – has driven up prices.

“[The price of a board has] increased because of the blockade, from about 35 shekels ($11) to 200 shekels ($60). Demand rose within a short period, but the available quantities are very limited,” he says.

Adas says a more affordable small foldable chessboard that sold for about 25 shekels ($8) before the war now costs between 180 ($54) and 200 shekels ($60) or more.

While prices remain a great barrier for people in Gaza, where nearly the entire 2.3 million population has fallen below the poverty line, the growth of Stalemate has seen more people buy boards for their homes.

For those who cannot afford these prices, online platforms such as Chess.com and Lichess have become popular to allow them to play against opponents outside Gaza. But power cuts and poor internet connectivity are other issues they face.

Adas hopes to secure a safe and permanent venue where players can train and compete free of charge. She also wants to create more opportunities for girls and women so they can go on and represent Palestine in international tournaments in the future.

For now, players continue meeting at chess gatherings which move between locations each week, offering a safe space for people to connect after enduring huge personal losses and hardship during the genocide.

“The return of chess is an act of defiance against the harsh circumstances,” al-Masri, the federation spokesperson, said.

pending_items.title: Yemen government forces hit Houthi positions as UN warns of hunger crisis
pending_items.content:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have launched multiple air strikes across Houthi-held territory, with at least 121 Houthis killed or injured over the past day.

Reporting from the capital, Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said on Saturday that more than six Yemeni governorates were hit overnight by the Saudi-led coalition, which backs the government forces.

“In the capital, Sanaa, 13 people were injured, including three critically, who were rushed to a hospital after a gas station was hit in the Tahrir district. The attack also hit homes and shops,” he said.

The second air attack in Sanaa, according to the Houthis, killed a man and his wife after it hit their home, he added.

He also listed an attack on a fuel station in the district of Bani Matar, on the outskirts of Sanaa, a raid on the southern city of Taiz and five air raids in the strategic city of Mocha, along the Red Sea coastline, which targeted a power station.

The “Dawn of Yemen” government offensive comes as fighting has escalated in Yemen in the past months, with Saudi-led coalition forces ramping up operations against the Houthis.

Military spokesman Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said earlier on Friday that government forces carried out 726 attacks against Houthi positions in the 24 hours prior, and claimed 121 fighters and commanders were killed or wounded. He added that fighting was ongoing in Ma’rib, al-Jawf, Taiz, Lahij, Shabwah, Midi and al-Dhale areas.

Houthi-affiliated media reported that a Saudi air strike killed 11 civilians, most of them children, in al-Turbah in Taiz governorate.

Al Jazeera could not confirm the death toll, and coalition forces did not comment.

Meanwhile, the government-run Saba news agency reported that Houthi attacks on government locations in Taiz on Saturday also resulted in the death of three civilians, including a 10-year-old boy. Three others, including an infant, were wounded.

Coalition officials added that a Houthi missile launched at Saudi Arabia’s capital Riyadh was intercepted and that Houthi attacks on government positions along the al-Masrakh district front, south of Taiz, were repelled.

The claims and casualties could not be independently verified.

Yemen has been racked by violence since the Iran-backed Houthis seized Sanaa and other parts of the country in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia to lead a military coalition in support of the internationally recognised government in March 2015.

Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis resumed in July amid tensions surrounding the US-Israel war on Iran, and after a 2022 ceasefire collapsed.

The renewed violence has worsened an ongoing humanitarian crisis, with thousands displaced and the prices of food, fuel and other necessities soaring.

Aid groups warn the crisis has been deepened by dramatic aid cuts by donors like the United States and other Western countries in the past year.

The World Food Programme and the Food and Agriculture Organization warned on Friday that Yemen is among nations facing the gravest risk of food insecurity, and that hunger is likely to worsen there over the next six months.

About 1.8 million people faced emergency levels of hunger in government-held areas, according to the agencies’ analysis. More than 300,000 people have been newly displaced since the escalation began, mostly in Taiz, Lahij and Aden provinces, the report said.

The encirclement of the city of Taiz has created conditions resembling a siege, it warned, adding that Houthi-held areas were becoming harder to access and monitor, and that the group was holding 73 UN staff.

The Houthis encircled Taiz city in early October.

A UN assessment earlier in February had found 18.3 million people across the country – more than half the population – were in crisis or worse.

pending_items.title: Why is Trump backing Iraq’s anti-smuggling campaign?
pending_items.content:
United States President Donald Trump has thrown his weight behind Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s campaign against oil smuggling. Baghdad has moved to take control of border crossings and oilfields in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region and has confronted Kataib Hezbollah, Iran’s most powerful armed ally in Iraq.

The endorsement came days before talks between Baghdad and Erbil are due to take place on December 1 under the sponsorship of the head of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council.

In a post on Truth Social on Friday, Trump wrote: “We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state.

“We support Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s efforts to build a united, prosperous, and strong Iraq that makes its own political decisions,” he added.

The post marked Washington’s first comment on tensions between Baghdad and Erbil. On Tuesday, al-Zaidi moved to place the Kurdish region’s border crossings and several oilfields under federal control. On Wednesday, Iraq’s top court ruled that Baghdad can deploy federal forces along all of the country’s international borders, including those of the Kurdish region. On Thursday, Iraq closed two crossings in the region, one with Syria and one with Iran.

Salim Zakhour, a researcher specialising in constitutional law and political systems, told Al Jazeera that the timing is significant, as Trump’s post comes after Baghdad’s measures and before the planned dialogue meeting.

“It is a clear message, first to the federal government, as a show of support for it,” he said. “But the more important message is for the authorities and Kurdish leaders in the Kurdistan region. It tells them that all the measures taken by the federal government have strong American backing.”

The Iraqi government says it wants to clamp down on oil smugglingو which is harming its economy.

The campaign began in Jurf al-Sakhar , also known as Jurf al-Nasr, a town in Babil province south of Baghdad. The armed group Kataib Hezbollah has held the town since 2014, when Iran-backed groups took it from ISIL (ISIS), and its mostly Sunni residents were displaced.

Senior Iraqi security, army, police and oil officials told the Reuters news agency that Kataib Hezbollah has since run an oil smuggling network there, siphoning off state-owned crude worth hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021.

Nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed and referred to the courts . Kataib Hezbollah, which the US designates as a “terrorist” organisation, denies the allegations .

Al-Zaidi gave the group until November 20 to leave the town. A day before the deadline, the two sides reached a compromise , reportedly following direct intervention by Esmail Qaani, the head of Iran’s Quds Force.

Under the deal, government forces entered Jurf al-Sakhar and set up a joint operations centre. Kataib Hezbollah units are due to withdraw gradually as army, federal police, energy police and Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) units deploy in phases.

Kataib Hezbollah is not the only group resisting Baghdad’s push to bring weapons under state control. Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have also refused to disarm . After the armed groups missed a September 30 deadline to hand over their weapons to the state, the government pushed the deadline to June 2027 .

Baghdad then extended the campaign to the Kurdish region. Government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that Iraq has lost an estimated $100bn between 2008 and 2025 from oil smuggled through the region. Reuters reported that it was unclear how that figure had been calculated.

Kurdish region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani called the measures unconstitutional and rejected them outright. Thousands of Kurds protested on Thursday, although Kurdish officials have said they do not want clashes with Baghdad and have left the door open to talks.

Liqaa Makki, a senior researcher at the Al Jazeera Centre for Studies, said Baghdad turned to the Kurdish region before the Jurf al-Sakhar operation was finished.

“The forces went in, but what next? There were promises that residents would return, that the town would be rebuilt and that Kataib Hezbollah would leave. None of that has happened,” he said.

Makki said al-Zaidi was responding to Shia armed groups asking why Baghdad was targeting them and not the Kurds, and wanted to show them “I am tough with everyone.”

He added that the prime minister could exploit divisions within the Kurdish region between the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan, based in Sulaimaniyah, and Erbil. “This is a good opportunity, because Sulaimaniyah is with him against Erbil,” he said.

Ghalib al-Daami, an academic and political researcher in Baghdad, told Al Jazeera that the Federal Supreme Court has already settled the legal question about borders with the Kurdish region.

“The border crossings, in terms of control, are run by the federal government, which also sets fiscal policy, but the actual day-to-day management of the crossings is to be joint,” he said. That would mean federal forces working alongside local Kurdish forces, such as the Asayish and the police.

“Oil, as interpreted by the Federal Court and the Iraqi constitution, is the property of all Iraqis,” he added.

“Very,” Muhanad Seloom, a senior non-resident fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera. “It is Iran’s main land outlet under blockade.”

Seloom said Iraqi buyers imported about $11.9bn of Iranian goods in 2024, one-fifth of Iran’s non-oil exports. “Gas for Iraqi power plants adds $4-5bn a year, and Iraqi banks give Tehran a route around sanctions,” he said.

Iraq is one of Iran’s most important economic partners. Bilateral trade topped $10bn in 2025, according to Iraqi official figures, driven mainly by Iranian exports of food and consumer goods. Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization put the figure at about $11.6bn.

Energy is at the centre of the relationship. According to US Energy Information Administration data, Iranian gas fuels power plants that produce 30 to 40 percent of Iraq’s electricity.

Iraq has also served as a channel for Iran to get around sanctions. Reuters revealed in late 2024 that a fuel oil smuggling network in Iraq was generating at least $1bn a year for Iran and its allies.

That channel has become more valuable as pressure on Tehran has grown amid the US war. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports used for exporting oil and has threatened sanctions against countries and groups that continue doing business with Iran.

Washington also has unusual leverage over Baghdad because Iraq’s oil revenues are held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. In April, the US halted a $500m cash payment to Iraq to press Baghdad to take action against Iran-backed groups.

Seloom said the best-documented scheme involves Iranian oil that is relabelled as Iraqi. “US Treasury designations since July 2025 describe blending and forged papers, and in May the trail reached Iraq’s deputy oil minister,” he said.

He said a newer claim – that crude from Kirkuk and Sulaimaniyah is trucked into Iran – “rests on one intelligence document that AFP has viewed without being able to confirm, and Erbil rejects it.”

An Iraqi intelligence document cited by the state news agency INA suggests crude is being moved by tanker truck from oilfields in Kirkuk and Sulaimaniyah provinces into Iran. There, it is reportedly blended with Iranian oil and sent on to Afghanistan, in what the document describes as an effort to help Iran “evade sanctions”. The document also suggests there may be a second route via crossings into Turkiye.

Washington has made similar accusations for some time. In May, the US Department of the Treasury sanctioned Iraq’s deputy oil minister, Ali Maarij al-Bahadly, accusing him of abusing his position to divert oil for the benefit of Iran and its allied armed groups in Iraq. Earlier, the Treasury sanctioned a network of companies run by Iraqi businessman Salim Ahmed Said . It accused the network of blending Iranian oil with Iraqi oil and selling it as purely Iraqi.

Seloom said Iraq is “the land gap” in Trump’s blockade of Iran.

“Closing it costs him no troops,” he said. “The crackdown slots into Washington’s economic-blockade strategy. It also squeezes militia funding and shores up al-Zaidi.”

The security source in Baghdad told the AFP news agency that the crackdown has US backing as Washington seeks to limit Iran’s economy.

Zakhour said the US position on the Kurds has also shifted. Washington backed Kurdish autonomy for decades, from the no-fly zones of the 1990s to the decentralised federal system written into the 2005 constitution.

“Now there is a different approach, led by the US envoy to Iraq and Syria, Ambassador Tom Barrack,” he said. “This approach is towards more centralised decision-making, both in general and especially on investment and oil.”

He said Barrack’s view is that “when American companies sign contracts, there must be a single party to sign with, and there must be no disputes after the signing.

“Everything we are seeing now is aimed at securing that demand,” Zakhour added.

Makki said Washington’s backing has freed al-Zaidi to take on Erbil. “America is now standing behind him with all its strength,” he said. “So he is not afraid that the Americans will side with the Kurds. On the contrary, they are asking the Kurds to stand with al-Zaidi.”

Al-Daami rejected any suggestion that US backing compromises al-Zaidi, who has steered Iraq closer to Washington and whom Trump hosted at the White House in July this year.

“Fighting corruption, preventing smuggling and controlling national wealth are clearly a domestic agenda,” he said. “Yes, that agenda lines up with the American one.”

“Yes, but more as a launchpad than a battlefield,” Seloom said. “Militia participation in any renewed US-Iran round is very likely.”

He said Iraq has had no US troops present since September 30. “So I expect militia fire from Iraqi soil and US air strikes on militia leaders, not a ground war,” he said.

The risk is rising. The US and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28, and a ceasefire took effect following a memorandum of understanding in June. But that agreement, which would have paved the way to wider peace talks, fell apart, and the two sides have continued to exchange attacks in recent weeks, while the US blockades Iranian ports.

Trump has said he “would not hesitate” to resume full military strikes if diplomacy fails, and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has warned that Tehran will “rain down hell” if the US escalates.
